question: How does a still melody change when its accompaniment begins to flow?
intro: The third movement of Suite bergamasque begins with quiet, measured chords, not with the flowing accompaniment of its middle. Follow how that movement changes the atmosphere, then remains beneath the opening melody when it is recalled.

sections.label: A · Quiet chords
sections.mNote: paired melodic notes unfold above slow harmonic changes

sections.label: B · The flowing middle
sections.mNote: arpeggiated accompaniment supports a widening melodic line

sections.label: A′ · Quiet recollection
sections.mNote: the opening melody re-emerges above more mobile accompaniment

sections.label: Coda · Dying away
sections.mNote: flowing figures and sustained harmony recede towards the final tonic

cues.title: Stillness made from moving voices
cues.text: The opening melody often moves in paired notes above slow changes of harmony. Listen to the way those voices connect between chords: the quietness comes from sustained phrases, not from every part of the piano remaining motionless.
cues.evidence: Viewed Fromont score, plate E. 1404 F., printed p. 14: Andante très expressif, pp, 9/8 and paired upper notes over slow harmony. The report shows the restrained opening through 0:35. No individual note onset or pedal movement is claimed. Score: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=12015&itemFileId=27374
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Moonlight and masked dancers
cues.text: Verlaine’s 1869 poem of the same title places masked dancers, lute-playing and uncertain happiness in moonlight. Its first stanza names “bergamasques”. That literary world offers context for the suite’s titles, not a script assigning a particular image to every musical phrase.
cues.evidence: The poem’s 1869 publication is identified at https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Clair_de_lune_%28Verlaine%29. The opened 1891 Vanier text, pp. 5–6, supplies masks, bergamasques, lute, dancing and uncertain happiness: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/F%C3%AAtes_galantes_(1891)/Clair_de_lune. No literal musical depiction or bar-by-bar programme is asserted.

cues.title: Third of four movements
cues.text: The suite was begun in 1890 and revised before its 1905 publication. Clair de lune sits between the Menuet and Passepied, after the opening Prélude. Hearing it alone is a selection from that four-movement design, not a different one-piece suite.
cues.evidence: The 1905 Fromont score and Sibley catalogue give the four-movement order: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/institutionalPublicationPublicView.action?institutionalItemVersionId=11883. The composition and revision range is documented in the work catalogue: https://imslp.org/wiki/Suite_bergamasque_%28Debussy%2C_Claude%29.

cues.title: A current beneath the melody
cues.text: In the flowing middle, broken chords spread beneath longer melodic notes. Try holding the upper phrase in your attention while the accompaniment crosses the keyboard: greater activity below does not make every note of the tune equally hurried.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 15–17 supplies un poco mosso, rolling accompaniment and long upper phrases. The report finds a strong change at 1:26, quieter level around 1:30 and renewed swells around 1:40–1:50. These anchor a broad middle paragraph; no bar or measured local tempo is assigned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A swell, then less weight
cues.text: The middle’s fuller phrases eventually yield to calmer writing. Follow the reduction in weight without losing the moving accompaniment: it becomes the link back towards the opening’s quieter way of singing.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 16–18 moves through En animant, a fuller crest, dim. and Calmato before a Tempo I. The report has changes at 2:18 and 2:34, a stronger 2:25 window and a marked level drop after 2:30. This describes the surrounding withdrawal, not an exact Calmato onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One side of an HMV disc
cues.text: Moiseiwitsch recorded this performance at Abbey Road Studio 3 on 28 February 1946. HMV issued it as one side of C.3485, coupled with Chopin’s B♭ Polonaise, op. 71 no. 2. The matrix and take identify this performance more precisely than the work’s familiar title.
cues.evidence: The matching chronology entry BM-C#051 gives date, studio and matrix 2EA10890-1: https://classical-pianists.net/viii/benno-moiseiwitsch/chronology-2/. The original label and Internet Archive metadata identify C.3485 and the coupling: https://archive.org/metadata/78_clair-de-lune-moonlight_benno-moiseiwitsch-debussy_gbia3042373b/metadata. DAHR was consulted but no accessible matching entry was established.

cues.title: A memory with different support
cues.text: In the later recollection, compare the opening melody with its first appearance. The accompanying movement makes the familiar line feel less isolated. Recognition comes from the melodic shape, even though the surrounding piano texture has changed.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 18–19 restores a Tempo I and the opening melodic material over arpeggiated accompaniment. The report places the later paragraph at a substantially quieter level than the middle, with changes at 2:52 and 3:34. The cue concerns the return as a whole; it does not claim its first bar at 3:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Arrival before disappearance
cues.text: The closing instruction asks the sound to die away to the end. Listen for the difference between reaching a quiet harmonic resting place and the remaining piano resonance disappearing: the musical arrival does not have to be the last thing you hear.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p. 19 gives pp morendo jusqu’à la fin and the final D♭-major harmony. The report’s five-second levels fall from about 4:00 through the very quiet 4:15 window in this 259.9-second file. The final chord’s exact attack and pedal release are not separately timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Held chords open into moving accompaniment
transitions.how: The opening’s chordal phrases grow in register and weight, then diminish before un poco mosso introduces a more continuous current of broken chords. The upper melody can sustain longer notes while the lower part moves through the harmony. Debussy changes the texture and pace without abandoning the broad melodic line: the new activity is chiefly underneath it, and the middle subsequently carries that movement into a wider, more animated span.
transitions.evidence: Viewed Fromont score pp. 15–16 supplies the chordal build, dim. molto and un poco mosso with arpeggios. The report finds a strong boundary at 1:26 after the loud 1:20 window, followed by a much quieter 1:30 window. The boundary is an approximate passage estimate, not a bar alignment.

transitions.title: The flowing figure carries the memory back
transitions.how: The animated middle withdraws through Calmato: the accompaniment continues, but the line and dynamics become gentler. The ensuing a Tempo I recalls the opening melody in the upper register while keeping a more mobile accompaniment below. D♭ major again provides the home setting. The transition is therefore gradual: the moving figure survives the retreat and becomes the support for familiar material rather than disappearing at a hard boundary.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score pp. 17–18 supplies Calmato, the return to the five-flat signature and the ensuing a Tempo I with familiar melody and altered accompaniment. The report’s strongest change is at 2:34, after a 2:25 swell; 2:35–2:50 is markedly quieter. The section boundary groups the withdrawal and recollection. It does not claim that a Tempo I starts exactly at 2:34.

transitions.title: The returning phrase releases its remaining motion
transitions.how: The recalled melody gives way to the final flowing figures and sustained harmonies. Debussy marks the passage very quiet and dying away to the end, allowing D♭ major to settle without another large crest. The texture gradually leaves more room for resonance: movement becomes part of the release rather than the beginning of a fresh phrase.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score p. 19 supplies the final figures, pp morendo jusqu’à la fin and the D♭ close. Reported changes at 3:34, 3:40 and 3:50 anchor the closing region; levels decline strongly after 4:00. The 3:40 division is a passage-level coda estimate, not an exact first morendo note.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
